## 3. Wicker

**Score:** 105
**Body:** God save the English, who appear to be the only people who want to make sex comedies these days.  While it is true that Hollywood does release them occasionally, I can’t imagine a major studio doing anything remotely like *Wicker*.  Here’s a movie that is filthy and wickedly funny.  That the movie was independently produced and distributed by the new and small Black Bear, tells you everything about the meager choices moviegoers have for comedies these days.

I don’t want to characterize *Wicker* as a bawdy comedy, though, because the racy material really is a means to an end.  The movie is a variation on the “stranger comes to town” theme, with the stranger becoming the lens through which the townspeople’s actual feelings are brought to the surface and illuminated.  Imagine if Benny Hill directed *Chocolat* and you’ll get what *Wicker* is after.  While the ample sex jokes would have made Hill proud, they lead into moments of introspection and soulfulness that are surprisingly touching and moving.  (No, not like that.)

Aside from the dirty stuff, *Wicker* has a lot to say about marriage, trauma, jealousy and insecurity.  While its insights are familiar, the movie’s directness in conveying them makes them sticky.  For example, there’s a funny scene set in a tavern where the town’s husbands are upset over their wives demanding more in the marital bed since Mr. Wicker’s arrival.  It concludes with him asking one beleaguered husband if he loves his wife, a simple yet forthright question that causes him to break down crying.  (If you don’t grasp what that response implies, please see Mr. Wicker for counseling.)

To sell a strange story like this, having the right actors in key roles is critical.  Olivia Colman is perfectly cast as the Fisherwoman, a part that requires the incredible range she’s known for.  As Colman has proven in movies like *Wicked Little Letters*, *The Roses and The Favourite*, she’s an extremely capable comedian because she’s willing to do anything for a laugh.  This is a very unflattering role in many ways, and Colman spends a fair chunk of it looking like a slob.  But the role plays to Colman’s strengths because what matters to her is being convincingly vulnerable on screen.  She’s equally funny and touching in this movie, and proves why she’s one of the best actresses of her generation.

If you’re going to have a movie about a woman who falls in love with a man made out of wicker, it helps to have that man be played by Alexander Skarsgård.  He’s become the go-to actor for roles that allow the audience to project their fears and desires, and manages to make wicker sexy.  His performance is a tricky one, because he has to play Mr. Wicker as an innocent who gradually evolves into an introspective being.  Skarsgård acts as the straight man to all the crazy townspeople, the sole enlightened character in a sea of degenerates that also lacks situational awareness.  It’s a deft bit of acting that has become Skarsgård’s specialty.

Co-directors and screenwriters Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson had the right approach to this cracked fable.  They made the right call in grounding things in a setting that’s old-timey enough for the story, without fretting over period-specifics.  Fischer and Wilson’s direction has a grimy Monty Python quality to it, and nearly every joke lands.  The approach to the sex reminded me of *The Little Hours*, in how it implies much without being graphic.  For those who shudder at nudity, there is none here.  But if you watch it with your parents (or grandparents), you’re on your own.

The premise of *Wicker* sounds like a dirty joke you’d hear at a bar.  And while the movie resembles a reenactment of one at times, what makes it special is how philosophical it becomes.  Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård shine as the incredibly unlikely pairing that runs the emotional gamut.  **Recommended**.

More here:  [https://detroitcineaste.net/2026/11/03/wicker-movie-review-analysis-olivia-colman-alexander-skarsgard/](https://detroitcineaste.net/2026/11/03/wicker-movie-review-analysis-olivia-colman-alexander-skarsgard/)

## 4. I just watched signs....

**Score:** 56
**Body:** Always put it off because so many people said the ending is terrible. Absolutely fantastic movie and I can't believe I put it off for so long!  The reason I'm making the post is because Im genuinely confused about the criticism. People complain about the ending being stupid because it doesn't make any sense (I'm trying to write this without spoilers) but isn't the entire point of the movie that the aliens behave in a way that makes zero sense to us? It's a central part of the plot and subtext of the movie?

I'm just confused, am I missing something or did that many people genuinely not understand that that's the point?

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The point of the film has absolutely nothing to do with aliens at all and everything to do with what they talk about on the couch that night, best scene in the entire film. Brilliantly written 
  - So refreshing to see a movie talk about faith like this movie does. I'm not a faithful person myself, but you can't deny that it's a very important aspect of our history and how we got to where we are now. It's something modern art explores less and less
    - I love the theory that the movie is indeed ALL about faith, and the aliens are obviously demons. 

1-Dude is a priest. Movie literally ends with him regaining his faith and becoming a priest again. It's literally the moral of the story, lol.

2-The "aliens" have none of the traditional alien stuff in movies. Where are the spaceships in the sky? Not a single spaceship in the whole film? For an alien movie? No laser guns or anything like that.

3-The neighbor traps one in his closet. Sounds dumb, right? An advanced alien species, trapped in a closet. Until you realize the scene right before it is the neighbor explaining the grief he has carried and couldn't let go of. The alien represents what he has endured and hid for so many years.

4-The "aliens" are eventually thwarted with 'water'. Again, sounds like a plot hole until you realize that represents "holy water". The water left around the house by the daughter, who is literally called an "angel" in the film.

5-Near the end, when speaking of the solution that defeats them, there is even a reference to it coming out of the Middle East/Israel.

6-The main monologue and quote of the film from Gibson's character, that explains it all: 

>“People break down into two groups. When they experience something lucky, group number one sees it as more than luck, more than coincidence. **They see it as a sign, evidence, that there is someone up there, watching out for them.** Group number two sees it as just pure luck. Just a happy turn of chance.   
I'm sure the people in group number two are looking at those fourteen lights in a very suspicious way. For them, the situation is a fifty-fifty. Could be bad, could be good. But deep down, they feel that whatever happens, they're on their own. And that fills them with fear. Yeah, there are those people. But there's a whole lot of people in group number one. When they see those fourteen lights, they're looking at a miracle. And deep down, they feel that whatever's going to happen, there will be someone there to help them. And that fills them with hope. See what you have to ask yourself is what kind of person are you? **Are you the kind that sees signs, that sees miracles?** Or do you believe that people just get lucky? Or, look at the question this way: Is it possible that there are no coincidences?”

For most people, that quote is pretty on the nose. It literally uses the very title of the film, making it clear we are speaking of supernatural and spiritual signs, not aliens. 

People are free to have different opinions, as it's just a movie. But for me it seems pretty intentional. 

If it's strictly an alien film, it does have quite a few plot-holes and odd choices. If it's a semi-religious film focusing on demons, under the guise of an alien film(a type of twist that Shamylan is famous for), then it's a brilliant idea and presentation, imo.
      - “The "aliens" have none of the traditional alien stuff in movies. Where are the spaceships in the sky? Not a single spaceship in the whole film? For an alien movie? “

There is a spaceship. It’s shown on the TV when Merle is watching it. It’s over Mexico City, I believe. During the day it turns invisible but they know it’s still there because a flock of birds ran into it. And the aliens literally look like the stereotypical aliens: big heads, giant black eyes, green. 

I love the movie and like the demon theory, but your point number 2 doesn’t hold water. 
        - Y'know I do think that's a fair rebuttal. 

And while it'll probably sound like I'm trying to weasel out of the argument, I do think there are a few twists even with that one shot.

1-We only see twinkling "lights in the sky" in the clip.

2-The announcer does call them ufos, but again, that's the entire point of a twist, right? We are being told what the people in the story assume they are. The same way how in "The Village", the characters are constantly telling us 'errors' about the village that we eventually realize are not true.

3-Like with all of these, Shamylan seems to always put one little hint in there that it's not what it seems. In this case, the TV commentator noting that they "were not/cannot be picked up on radar". Again, if this is a straight/no twist alien flick, we assume, "oh they aliens just have cool tech". If it's a Shamylan twist, then you realize the entire point is these are not in fact some physical, metal, flying objects, but some kind of non physical entity that can be seen.

4-The "twinkling lights" in the sky are reminiscent to how the holy books described the devil and his angels(demons) as "falling either like lightning or stars from heaven".

5-Again, as much as I belabor my answer, I do think your argument is 100% valid. The reason I push back at all, is because if there was like that one bright silver, traditional alien spaceship coming down from the sky "movie shot" in the film, I do think I'd say the entire 'demon theory' is wrong. The mere "lights in the sky" clip isn't enough for me personally, and even it seems to hold up to the demon theory imo. 

Again, apologies if this sounded argumentative. I enjoy talking these various theories.
2. It’s “cool” to dunk on a director’s work instead of admitting the it’s fun to suspend disbelief and just roll with a fantastic movie. I personally love it 
3. People expect "signs" to mean signs of alien life. Ultimately it means something else to the main characters. There's a difference between knowing something and having faith in something.
4. >isn't the entire point of the movie that the aliens behave in a way that makes zero sense to us?

ummm... no
5. It's an awesome movie, watching it as a kid, I thought it was just a good time but even rewatching it the extra layers make it even better

I mean that bit isn’t even an error really, it could show how desperate the aliens were to harvest other resources from our planet, if they came to a planet 2/3s of what they’re allergic to etc.   
good performances and great atmosphere can trump a couple of plot inconsistencies. 

## 5. Wild Horse Nine - Review

**Score:** 6
**Body:** **It brings me no joy to say that this is probably my biggest disappointment of the year.**

**Full review:** [**https://widescreenmemory.wordpress.com/2026/11/03/wild-horse-nine-review/**](https://widescreenmemory.wordpress.com/2026/11/03/wild-horse-nine-review/)

At the heart of *Wild Horse Nine* is a film that finds itself somewhere between two of Martin McDonagh’s previous works: *In Bruges* and *The Banshees Of Inisherin*. Fundamentally, this is a film where a central character must come to terms with the meaning of their own existence and inherent mortality. Unfortunately, *Wild Horse Nine* fails where *In Bruges* and *The Banshees of Inisherin* also succeeded, namely in creating a world around this central concept. The result is a film that frustratingly feels less than the sum of its part.

At the centre of it all is John Malkovich, delivering what might well be the finest performance of his career. Now I’ve always found Malkovich to be an actor who has often made a living out of playing variations of himself, leaning into that wonderfully eccentric screen persona that has become so recognisable. Here, however, there is something considerably more vulnerable at work. Yes, the Malkovich-isms are still present, but his deep sense of interiority provides the film with its most affecting moments, and some of McDonagh's best writing. It's a performance of remarkable subtlety, and one that reminds you just how extraordinary an actor Malkovich can be when given the opportunity to step outside his usual comfort zone. It also serves to remind us that McDonagh is exceptionally gifted at pulling out career-best performances from veteran actors (see Frances McDormand in *Three Billboards*).

The broader political backdrop should, in theory, provide plenty of material for McDonagh to get his teeth into. CIA agents operating in Chile, with their involvement in the country's descent into fascism, is an inherently fascinating premise. Yet the film never does anything particularly interesting with this historical context, instead diverting into another, rather strange and distracting theory about CIA involvement. It's an odd narrative detour that ultimately detracts from what is already a film struggling to establish exactly what it wants to say.

This is where the real disappointment of *Wild Horse Nine* lies. *In Bruges* and *The Banshees Of Inisherin* were both films that had wonderful core relationships and ideas, but they were enhanced through the worlds in which they operated in, and ultimately were synonymous with one another. Yet *Wild Horse Nine*’s world feels oddly distanced from its core characters. Attempts at broader political ideas feel extremely surface-level and reveal that McDonagh’s strengths as a writer lie primarily in his characters, not his ability to convey political ideas. As such, it feels like Lee and Chris’ story could have taken place anywhere and at anytime, whereas you felt that the stories of *In Bruges* and *The Banshees Of Inisherin* could only take place within their time and place.

There is a brilliant performance from Malkovich, some excellent filmmaking and enough flashes of McDonagh's distinctive voice to make this worthwhile. But too much of what surrounds those elements feels superfluous, and I couldn't shake the feeling that there was a considerably better version of this film, but ultimately one that I had seen before from McDonagh. A frustratingly middling effort from a filmmaker capable of so much more.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. There seems to be a new American cinematic movement emerging

**Score:** 156
**Body:** Well into the second half of the 2020s, the defining independent film movement of the decade is making itself apparent. I might call it “new weird America” if that wasn’t already a thing. It seems to have coalesced around the late 2010s (the earliest definitive example I can think of is DRM’s excellent *Under the Silver Lake*) as a response to developments in American culture and society. A few key stylistic devices appear ubiquitous: worship of Kaufman & the Coen bros, absurdist satire of social media and internet culture, nightmare worst-case-scenario plots, irreverent inclusion of magical realism & metafiction, heavy emphasis on black humor and “cringe comedy”, and suggestions of an unseen omnipresent malevolent force at the heart of it all.

Though *Digger* and *Eddington* were enough to prove that most audiences won’t find this bizarre brand of social commentary palatable, their thread has been creeping its way into the mainstream, slowly establishing itself as a major ideological influence on American pop culture (when I saw *Obsession*, I was especially struck by its similarities to *The Curse* in its attitude towards the supernatural). This movement seems especially modern in its rejection of the distinction between the different forms of cinematic art—note how many of its main auteurs (Nathan Fielder, Connor O’Malley, Tim Robinson) seem to be equally comfortable in the fields of film, television, and internet video. Another interesting feature of the style is a kind of giddy excitement towards the act of constructing the film itself: the numerous visual callbacks that constitute the mystery of *Under the Silver Lake*, the epic five-act structure of *Beau is Afraid*, the wild imagination of *The Rehearsal*, the many stylistic shifts in *Coreys,* etc.

I'm sure that what I've identified is just the most recent era in a much older broader tradition in cinema, but I bring up these films and filmmakers specifically because they seem to have a head on their shoulders in a way that I don't see in a lot of other modern filmmakers, especially when it comes to dealing with modern issues. Would love to hear thoughts or suggestions

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Silverlake and Eddington in particular are very pynchon-esque. I think this movement is in part a resurgence of 60s/70s beat and psychedelic literary sensibilities. Stuff like Pynchon, DeLillo, Tom Robbins, Terry Southern. Boots Riley's works are aligned with this register. I think Sinners fits the bill too. It's a use of genre as device rather than aesthetic - combined with an underlying sense of the mythic. 
  - *One Battle After Another*, being based on *Vineland*, is an obvious point in case
  - We had great Pynchon and Delillo adaptations in the first half of the 2010s with Inherent Vice and Cosmopolis. Both really underrated in their day, interestingly. I think they’d be much more warmly received right now.
  - Speaking of Pynchon, you also have Paul Thomas Anderson's two actual Pynchon adaptations (2014 & 25).
  - This movement needs a catchy name.
    - I mean, it’s just literary post-modernism, which didn’t really have a mainstream moment in film. Call it neo-post-modernism, call it post modernism revival. 
      - They said "catchy"

Most of the films you mention, I've enjoyed, but not sure about them being part of a trend. The argument seems to become circular: films are grouped because they share certain characteristics, then the existence of the group is used as evidence that those characteristics define a new movement.

Instead, maybe it's this. Some of today's filmmakers are reviving the paranoid social satire of the 1960s–70s, the surreal nightmare comedy of the 1980s, and the metafictional experiments of the 1990s, now filtered through internet culture.

* Absurdism, paranoid conspiracies, nightmare scenarios, black comedy, metafiction, magical realism (and characters trapped in incomprehensible systems) have been part of cinema for decades. Citing Kaufman and the Coens seems to undermine the argument. If the defining characteristics of a new movement are principally the characteristics of earlier filmmakers, what's actually new?

* Films like Under the Silver Lake, Beau Is Afraid, Eddington, The Rehearsal, and Obsession are quite different from each other. One can make them sound like a single movement through selective description, but their narrative approaches, purposes, and even their relationships with reality are pretty different.

* Social media, influencers, online conspiracies, and internet culture are contemporary subjects. That doesn't make the cinematic methods used to satirize them new. Previous generations made similar films about television, advertising, corporate culture, mass surveillance, and consumerism. Replacing television with TikTok doesn't necessarily constitute a new movement.

* It's selection bias to start with an assortment of films you admire, identify their shared characteristics only, and then describe those characteristics as ubiquitous. What proportion of contemporary independent films actually exhibit these traits?

* What suggests there is a movement here, rather than parallelism? A recognizable film movement usually has some combination of shared artistic principles, mutual influence, collaborators, production methods, institutions, or a common cultural identity. And including Digger (a WB film w/ Tom Cruise and directed by an established international filmmaker) in an American independent film movement? What does independent mean in this argument?

* The suggestion that Digger and Eddington demonstrate how distasteful this style is to general audiences is a strange supporting argument. A film flopping can reflect its marketing, subject matter, reviews, or simply the film itself. A couple of divisive releases don't establish the significance of a movement, or a growing ideological influence on popular culture.

* The act of constructing the film mentioned (elaborate structures, visual callbacks, shifting styles, and deliberate narrative games) is almost a definition of postmodern cinema. Filmmakers were calling attention to the artificiality of storytelling decades before Under the Silver Lake. And, intricate construction isn't automatically evidence that a film has something worthwhile to say. A filmmaker can be extraordinarily clever without being particularly perceptive.

The films I'd consider:

    The President's Analyst (1967)
    Putney Swope (1969)
    O Lucky Man! (1973)
    Network (1976)
    Brazil (1985)
    Repo Man (1984)
    After Hours (1985)
    The Truman Show (1998)
    Being John Malkovich (1999)
    Southland Tales (2006)

Those films are predate the films listed in the OP, and provide a clear counter-argument.

Here are more specific ones, counter-examples to example:

    The Trial (1962)
    Barton Fink (1991)
     -> Beau Is Afraid

    The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (1972)
    The King of Comedy (1982)
     -> The Curse

    The Parallax View (1982)
    The Player (1992)
     -> Under the Silver Lake

Nathan Fielder, Connor O'Malley, and Tim Robinson do represent a creative environment in which the divisions between sketch comedy, YouTube, television, and feature filmmaking are less important. But Monty Python moved between television, film, comedy albums, and live performance. The earlier careers of Albert Brooks, Andy Kaufman, and Robert Downey Sr. also demonstrate a similar willingness to ignore distinctions between media.

Basically, take The President's Analyst (1967), Brazil (1985), and Southland Tales (2006). Those three films demonstrate the entire aesthetic described above as having existed in earlier times.

## 2. Videodrome (1983)

**Score:** 55
**Body:** Videodrome (1983)  
Rating: 9/10  
Watched: November 3, 2026

I guarantee you I saw this movie when I was no older than 12 or 13. And that is *genuinely* too young for a Cronenberg movie in general and *super too young* for Videodrome. I had no idea what I was watching in the specific scope of the movie's plot and themes, but not too young to think 'what in the actual hell is this' every few minutes once Videodrome gets rolling.

There's something almost insufferably seedy about Max Renn, and quite possibly even James Woods himself in this movie. The last time I watched Videodrome was probably well over 20 years ago, and back then I was still pretty much 'Cronenberg sexy body horror Debbie Harry topless' and I make no apologies for it, but now, at 54?

Max Renn is a skeevy perv. *Skeevy*. He reminds me somehow of Ratso Rizzo in just his oily grossness. He feels like the sort of guy who'd grope a girl on the subway and pretend nothing was happening.

Max's descent into what I can only describe as hallucinatory carnal madness as he chases ever more visceral pleasures is something else. He becomes feverish as the lines between what's real and what's in the eternal broadcast really does become quite freaky.

One of my most favorite things about this movie is Brian O'Blivion's whole rap. I used to run around talking about cathode ray tubes and the eternal signal and being very specifically weird about it. The problem with this is I was the only thirteen in probably a 10 mile radius that'd ever *seen* Videodrome. At 54, I still love the whole crazed concept of the lines between fiction and reality blurring in this way; half-prophet, half-loon, O'Blivion's monologues 'speak to me'.

That's fully trite, I suppose, but it's true all the same, and I do think that's more or less the point behind that whole side of things. It's *meant* to lure you in.

The other thing (naturally) when it comes to a Cronenberg movie is that good old-fashioned body horror. The man had a knack for creating some of the most disturbing concepts in the world *and* getting his prop/effects team to bring every single one of them to life.

13 year old me was grossed out in that weird titillated way only seriously weird kids could be by nudity, the general filthy shabbiness of Max's chosen profession and things like the gun transformation as it weaves it's way directly into Max's hand towards the end of the movie.

54 year old me still loves all that, but after a lifetime of being enamored with skillful practical effects and being firmly on the side of 'practical is better than anything else', Videodrome's effects still somehow remain top shelf for me.

Videodrome isn't something you can idly sit down and decide to watch on a whim, and you sure can't doomscroll on your phone while it's playing. So much is going on under the surface, like a carrier wave (if you will) and to blink is to miss it.

As wide and varied as James Woods' career's been since Videodrome came out, his performance here as hungry Max Renn remains one of his best.
